comments.author: @cleverboyx
comments.text:
It is positively bizarre that someone would have the tone-deafness to say “If Google’s Youtube isn’t going to sue for copyright infringement, then what chance do a bunch of singer songwriters have”. I mean… take a pause and absorb that. This person is assuming GOOGLE is the copyright holder to its hosted material. And, considering the Viacom lawsuit that threatened to end Youtube early on prior to Google acquiring it, it just explodes my mind how ridiculous this statement is. I mean… yikes. 

Taking a step back, yes, the creators and musicians are concerned about people mass producing content with their voices and generated off of their music. It’s exceptionally reasonable that “training” off of existing work is problematic. Why is it problematic if humans have done it for ages? Because it is a “mechanical process”. Without the underlying work, the provenance is broken and the output doesn’t exist. Humans are privileged over machines. At least for now according to copyright laws. If a human significantly participated in a work, it is not a mechanically process and the human can claim a measure of copyright.

If YOUR work was used… your voice… your artwork… your visual appearance… to create a new work with NO authorship or copyright standing, why is it that you get no credit or usage rights?

These are the important questions. And the jury is kind of out on them. But, this tech bro attitude of “who are these singer songwriters… they are nothing… they need to go home…” needs to be stopped entirely. Respect should be paid. Not “overpaid”. The world can’t come to a stop. But, we need to paise. Because this literally is the future of how we develop as a species. Disincentivizing the creation of art or music or learning on any level (because Ai) is an exceptionally bad idea.

comments.author: @Darhan62
comments.text:
Training a model on copyrighted but publicly available data isn't the same as "storing" or "consuming" the data -- it's merely learning patterns in the data in a way that's analogous to how a human infant learns patterns in its sensory inputs and thus gains the skills of physical coordination, visual imagination, object permanence, understanding of its environment, etc...  Lawsuits based on a false understanding of how the models work and what training a model actually entails are doomed to failure.

A lot of the people pushing back against AI training on copyrighted works are still stuck with the idea that the models are making collages out of artists' paintings or assembling new articles out of snippets of different authors' written works.  That understanding is totally off base.  I am concerned that politicians will try to appease their prospective voters by deliberately pretending to share their same misunderstanding of how the models work.

Full disclosure, I usually vote with the Democrats, but in California I could certainly imagine unscrupulous Democrats courting the votes of liberal Hollywood types and creatives by feeding their misunderstandings and Luddite fears.  Republicans do the same kind of thing and worse on other issues.  I am concerned about regulatory capture by the larger companies.  Much of what's going on right now with lawsuits and politicians talking about AI regulation is performative -- a dog and pony show.

The copyright question, is not so much about scanning publically available images or videos, although the likes of Youtube will want to see it that way, but in the unfair advantage that AI brings to the table. 

Even if I had very little skills to create art myself, I could use AI to compensate for that. This means that the people who learned and practiced to get those skills, and produced that which AI learned from, are not compensated fairly for all the time and effort that resulted in being able to create the sources that AI has scanned.
